title: I spent months using AI coding agents almost 24/7 on a huge solo RPG. Today its biggest update ships: here's what that workflow actually looked like
author: SevenWeeksStudios
selftext:
Hi! I've been developing games for a few years, but until this year I had never managed to get anywhere close to actually releasing something publicly.

The thing is, once you have a job, a kid and a family, it becomes very difficult to balance all of that with game development, as I imagine many of you here know very well!

But with the rise of AI, earlier this year I started using agents to help me. At first, it was just a test to see how far they could actually help, but as I kept sending prompts, testing and playing, the project kept growing and growing without really stopping, until I reached the last month, when I decided to push things as far as I could.

I used the money I had made from my game's first month of sales to subscribe to Claude Max and ChatGPT Pro for one month. The problem is that, as I said above, I don't have much free time, so I had to optimize my workflow as much as possible.

Usually, my son would go to sleep at around 8 PM, and then I would stay up playing the game, taking notes and talking to a ChatGPT agent that helped me organize my ideas until around 1 AM, sometimes earlier if I was too tired.

With those notes, I would describe to the agents what I wanted them to do, trying to make the most out of what each one could contribute to the game. Then I would leave them working during the night.

When I woke up, I would review what they had changed and the results they reported, asking for screenshots whenever something seemed wrong and asking for confirmation through tests. Based on that, I would send more prompts and then go to work.

Once I had remote access to both agents, I was basically working from work lol. I would keep an eye on both agents while they worked on what I had asked, and again, I would request adjustments and corrections whenever I thought something was wrong. Then I would come home, play the game again, take more notes, and repeat the cycle.

I stayed in this workflow for almost every day of the month.

Astra seemed better to me when I needed better interpretation of what I was asking for. It seemed better at understanding points that I may have left a little vague.

Claude, especially after the release of Opus 5.5, seemed better to me when I made it very clear what I wanted. A lot of the time, I had to keep an eye on things, checking the images it sent me and making small adjustments along the way.

In the end, since I now have to choose one of them to continue using, I chose Claude. Opus 5.5 was great for me, and another factor is that Astra burns through credits extremely fast, so it just wouldn't work for me.

Another thing I learned: at first, I was a little obsessive about asking one model to write prompts for the other. But eventually I realized that writing directly to the specific model you want to use works much better, as long as you are very clear about what you want and how safe or conservative you want the implementation to be.

When one agent writes a prompt for another, it tends to assume intermediate steps or decisions that you don't necessarily agree with. And sometimes that ends up making you lose more time than you save.

The game is Morhval: Ravenglaire, a large old-school open-world RPG I've been building as a solo developer.

The game is currently 25% off on Steam, if anyone is interested.

If you have any questions, I'll be happy to answer when I can!
